papers.title_in_file: Image Classification using EmuCore - Quantum Computing Inc
papers.what_it_is: A vendor application page (a Jupyter-style walkthrough) in which Quantum Computing Inc classifies MNIST digits by passing flattened images through its EmuCore reservoir and fitting a linear model to the responses.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dataset consists of 70,000 images of handwritten digits 0-9, with 60,000 samples used for training and the remaining 10,000 images kept for testing, and that each sample is a 28 x 28 pixel image.
quotes: The dataset consists of 70,000 images of handwritten digits 0-9; 60,000 samples are used for training and the remaining 10,000 images are kept for testing.
Each sample is a 28 x 28 pixel image.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states its own dataset and split in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that the training data are imported with the mnist package from tensorflow, and the conclusion names the data as the MNIST digit dataset.

quotes: We use the mnist package from tensorflow to import training data.
build an image classification model using the MNIST digit dataset

assertions.value: The authors state that the images are serialized in one of the two spatial directions and sent through EmuCore, and that the output is an enriched dataset which is then used to train a simple linear model.
quotes: The images are serialized in one of the two spatial directions and sent through EmuCore.
The output is an enriched dataset which is then used to train a simple linear model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page describes its own pipeline in the Introduction and the code that follows.
assertions.reader_inference: Only the linear readout is trained; the reservoir is a fixed feature map, the usual reservoir computing arrangement. The page does not call it that in this paragraph.

assertions.value: The authors state that pixel values (integers from 0 to 255, representing 256 colors) are normalized to a 0-1 range, and claim that this normalization improves the behavior of the reservoir. The page shows no comparison without normalization.
quotes: The elements of the matrix are integers between 0 and 255, each representing one of the 256 colors.
We can normalize values to a 0-1 range. This normalization improves the behavior of the reservoir.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a measurement in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the flattening can be done in either of the two spatial directions, and claim that they tested both and the results are nearly identical. The page shows the results for one direction only (the swapaxes lines are commented out in the code).

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the other direction is not shown in the page.

papers.version_note: Web lesson page (Quantum Computing Inc), copyright line 2018-2026; no page breaks in the text layer, so read as one page.
papers.what_it_is: A vendor tutorial that explains optimization with a fence-and-garden example and solves it on the Dirac-3 entropy quantum computing device through the qci_client API.

assertions.value: The authors state that entropy quantum computing (EQC) is an analog quantum computing paradigm for optimization.
quotes: Entropy quantum computing (EQC) is an analog quantum computing paradigm for optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product category.

assertions.value: The authors state that Dirac-3 uses qudit variables, which take more than two values, so it can solve problems beyond binary, including integers and continuous numbers (all positive real rational numbers).
quotes: Unlike qubits, qudits can take more than two possible values. This means that Dirac-3 can solve problems beyond binary (0,1), including integers and continuous numbers (all positive real rational numbers).
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own device.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated variable domain is the positive real numbers only; negative values are not covered by the quoted statement.

assertions.value: The authors define optimization as searching for the best solution from a range of options. They call the goal the objective function, or in physics-oriented literature energy, and they define constraints as rules or limitations such as budget restrictions, time limits, or fuel constraints.
quotes: Optimization starts with identifying goals: searching for the best solution from a range of options
These goals are often referred to as the objective function, and less commonly in more physics oriented literature, energy.
Constraints are the rules or limitations, such as budget restrictions, time limits, or fuel constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own terms in the section What Is Optimization.

assertions.value: The authors state that Dirac-3 is like having a genius mathematician working for the user, ensuring good choices and saving time, energy, and resources.

assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product; the paper offers no evidence for it.
assertions.reader_inference: The page reports no benchmark, timing or comparison with another solver, so this is marketing language and not a measured result.

assertions.value: The paper sets a worked example: 100 ft of wire fencing for the three free sides of a rectangular garden against a rock wall, with the task of finding the dimensions of maximum area. The constraint is 2x + y = 100, where x is the side perpendicular to the wall and y the side parallel to it.
quotes: Given 100ft of wire fencing, determine the dimensions that would create a garden of maximum area.
Therefore, the constraint equation is 2 x + y = 100.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own example problem and constraint.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper borrows the example from a calculus textbook (Stewart, via LibreTexts), so the problem has a known closed-form answer.

assertions.value: The authors state that EQC devices aim to find the global minimum, so the maximization problem is negated and rewritten as a minimization problem.
quotes: The objective of EQC devices is to find the global minimum, representing the lowest values.
we need to negate the equation:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how it sets up its own problem for the device.

assertions.value: The authors state that Dirac-3 takes an Ising Hamiltonian up to fifth order as input and determines the lowest energy state. The paper writes the objective with linear (C), quadratic (J), cubic (T), quartic (Q) and quintic (P) coupling terms.
assertions.anchor: Formulating our equation into Dirac-3, p.1
quotes: Dirac-3 takes an Ising Hamiltonian (up to fifth-order) as input and determines the lowest energy state.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own device input format.

assertions.value: The authors encode the garden problem with two variables and only quadratic terms, so no higher order couplings are needed, giving the linear vector C = [-100, 0] and the coupling matrix J = [[2, 0], [0, 0]].
assertions.anchor: Formulating our equation into Dirac-3, p.1
quotes: Since our problem only involves quadratic terms, we do not need higher order couplings
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own encoding of the example.
assertions.reader_inference: The second variable carries only zero coefficients; the paper does not say in this lesson why it is needed beyond the hardware sum constraint.

assertions.value: The authors state that the second variable is included because of an additional constraint on the problem information that comes from the way the hardware is designed, known as a sum constraint. They defer the details to the Dirac-3 quick start.
assertions.anchor: Formulating our equation into Dirac-3, p.1
quotes: The reason relates to an addtional constraint on the problem information from the way the hardware is designed
known as a "sum constraint"

papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc. web tutorial page that explains combinatorial hardness, the traveling salesperson problem, P versus NP and approximate optimization, and positions the vendor's entropy quantum computing devices as solvers.

assertions.value: The authors (Quantum Computing Inc.) state that the problems their entropy quantum computing devices aim to solve are known as combinatorial optimization problems.
quotes: The problems which our entropy quantum computing devices aim to solve are known as combinatorial optimization problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of the target problem class of its own product.

assertions.value: The page defines combinatorial optimization problems as a class of optimization problems that are hard specifically because there are many potential solutions but no apparent practical way to find the best solution.
quotes: These are a class of optimization problems that are hard specifically because there are many potential solutions but no apparent practical way to find the best solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page's own definition of the term, given in its opening paragraph.

assertions.value: The authors state that for such problems it is easy to check the quality of a potential solution, but there are so many potential solutions that checking them all would be unreasonable for large instances, a combinatorial explosion that grows very fast with the number of variables.
quotes: For such problems, it is easy to check the quality of a potential solution, but there are many potential solutions, such that checking them all would be unreasonable for large instances.
the space of potential ways to solve the problem grows very fast
assertions.certainty_reason: A general tutorial statement without proof in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that such problems can be solved by enumeration, scoring each potential solution one at a time and comparing it to the best found so far, but that this can be infeasible in practice because the number of possible solutions can easily exceed large numbers such as the number of atoms in the universe.
quotes: Mathematically speaking, such problems can be solved by enumeration;
the number of possible solutions can easily exceed "large" numbers, like the number of atoms in the universe.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general tutorial statement without proof in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the simplest traveling salesperson problem, where a salesperson visits n cities, returns to the start and may use any order, there are (n-1)! possible routes because the starting point is fixed, and that adding one more city multiplies the number of potential routes by n.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, traveling salesperson example, p.1
quotes: a salesperson must visit a number of cities n n n , return to the city they started, and can do so in any order.
possible routes (since the starting point is fixed), and adding one more city would multiply the number of potential routes by n n n
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting statement given in a tutorial without a derivation; the formula is printed in the text layer in duplicated form.
assertions.reader_inference: The count (n-1)! is the standard number of orderings with a fixed start; the printed formula is garbled by the text layer but reads (n-1)! = (n-1)(n-2)...

assertions.value: The authors state that the factorial function which defines the number of routes explodes quickly, in fact faster than exponentially.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, traveling salesperson example, p.1
quotes: The factorial function which defines the number of cities explodes quickly, (in fact, faster than exponentially).
assertions.certainty_reason: Tutorial statement without proof in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page words this as the factorial 'which defines the number of cities'; the context shows it means the number of routes.

assertions.value: The authors give route counts for small traveling salesperson instances when a route and its reverse are treated as equivalent: four cities have 6 potential routes with a fixed start, of which only three need checking; five cities need 12 routes checked; six cities need 60 routes checked.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, traveling salesperson example, p.1
quotes: For four cities, there will only be 6 6 6 potential routes (recall the starting city is fixed)
only three routes would need to be checked
For five cities, 12 12 12 routes would need to be checked
For six cities 60 60 60 routes would need to be checked
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrative counts in a tutorial, stated without derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: The counts match (n-1)!/2 for four, five and six cities taken as n, so they are internally consistent with the stated formula and the reversal observation.

assertions.value: The authors state that for 11 cities millions of routes would have to be checked, which is doable, but for 21 cities over a billion times a billion routes would need to be checked, which is not feasible.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, traveling salesperson example, p.1
quotes: For 11 11 11 cities millions of routes would have to be checked (doable), but for 21 21 21 , over a billion times a billion would need to be checked (not feasible).
assertions.certainty_reason: Order-of-magnitude illustration in a tutorial, without derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: Consistent with the stated formula: 10!/2 is about 1.8 million and 20!/2 is about 1.2 times ten to the 18th, i.e. just over a billion times a billion.

assertions.value: The authors state that beyond the point where enumeration is feasible there are additional mathematical tricks that find the optimal route without enumerating all routes, by using the structure of the problem to prove that unchecked solutions must be less optimal than the one found; the page says these algorithms are not the topic of the tutorial.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, traveling salesperson example, p.1
quotes: They instead use the mathematical structure of the problem to prove that potential solutions that haven't been checked have to be less optimal than the one found.
Such strategies (i.e. algorithms) are very interesting, but not the topic of this tutorial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states what its tutorial does not cover, in the same paragraph.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is widely believed, although not strictly proven, that no matter how clever a strategy is, the time to find the most optimal route will always blow up with the size of the problem, and name this the famous P ≠ NP conjecture.
assertions.anchor: Combinatorial hardness, P versus NP paragraph, p.1
quotes: It is widely believed (although not strictly proven) that no matter how clever a strategy is, the time to find the most optimal route will always blow up with the size of the problem
This is the famous P ≠ N P P\neq NP P
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of a widely held belief about an open conjecture, attributed to common belief and not proven in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page presents the statement as a belief about the traveling salesperson problem; it is the usual statement of the conjecture applied to that problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that a large solution space is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a combinatorial optimization problem to be hard, because there also must be no known efficient strategy to solve the problem.
quotes: a large solution space is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for a combinatorial optimization problem to be hard
There also has to not be any known efficient strategy to solve the problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A tutorial statement without proof in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the shortest path problem has an exponentially growing number of possible solutions yet famous algorithms solve it quickly, because short paths between closer nodes can be built up into short paths between more distant nodes, whereas the traveling salesperson problem cannot be efficiently broken down in that way.
quotes: Some problems have an exponentially growing number of possible solutions, but there is an efficient way to find the optimal answer.
